questions.scenario: What is a 'control account' in the General Ledger?
options: An account only admins can view
A GL account whose balance must always equal the total of the subledger rows beneath it (e.g., 1310 Receivable—Export)
The account where differences are parked
A password-protected cash account
questions.explanation: The control account is the summary home of a subledger. Its single job: equal Σ(subledger detail) at all times — verified by reconciliation.
wrongExplanations: Access control is a security feature (Module 12), not what 'control account' means.
Parking differences there is exactly how mismatches get buried — the opposite of its purpose.
'Control' refers to summarizing-and-verifying, not security.

questions.scenario: Which question CANNOT be answered by the General Ledger alone?
options: Total receivables for the Balance Sheet
How much H&M owes on invoice INV-8901 specifically
Total payables balance
Cash at bank per the books
questions.explanation: Invoice-level, buyer-level, supplier-level, item-level questions belong to subledgers. The GL deliberately keeps one line per concept — that's why both layers exist.
wrongExplanations: Totals are exactly what the GL is for.
Correct: no invoice rows live in the GL — look in the AR subledger.
Control accounts hold these totals fine.

questions.scenario: AR subledger totals ৳8.5 crore; GL control account shows ৳8.2 crore. The professionally correct first action:
options: Post a ৳30 lakh journal to the GL to force equality
Report the GL figure as final since it feeds statements
Investigate document trails for postings missing from one layer (payments applied to GL but not buyer rows, manual journals without subledger rows, duplicates)
Average the two numbers and use ৳8.35 crore
questions.explanation: The difference IS the finding. You hunt the broken posting through documents until the gap is explained — then the fix makes both layers genuinely equal.
wrongExplanations: Forcing equality with an unexplained journal hides the error and breaks the audit trail — the classic unforgivable shortcut.
Neither number is presentable while unreconciled; the bank deserves the truth.
Averaging invented numbers creates a third wrong number.

questions.scenario: After GL and subledger disagree, what evidence-based rule should guide the correction?
options: The GL — because financial statements come from it
Neither automatically; use source documents, posting logs, and applications to identify which layer is wrong
Whichever number is larger
They are equally trustworthy always
questions.explanation: The detailed subledger is often the best starting trail, but it can also contain duplicates or errors. Evidence determines whether to correct the subledger, the GL, or both.
wrongExplanations: Statements inherit whatever the GL holds — inheritance doesn't make it true.
Size is not evidence; documents are.
Equality must be EARNED by reconciliation, not assumed.

questions.scenario: H&M pays ৳10,00,000 partially against invoice INV-8901 (৳12,40,000). What must the system write?
options: Only the GL entry Dr Bank / Cr Receivable
Only update the buyer's row in the AR subledger
Both atomically: GL entry Dr Bank ৳10,00,000 / Cr 1310 ৳10,00,000 AND the INV-8901 row updated to open ৳2,40,000
Reduce the invoice amount permanently to ৳10,00,000
questions.explanation: One payment event = one GL entry + its subledger application, written together or not at all. Partial payments leave the original amount intact with a smaller OPEN balance — history stays honest.
wrongExplanations: GL-only leaves the buyer row stale — instant mismatch.
Subledger-only leaves the GL stale — mismatch in the other direction.
Overwriting amounts destroys the audit trail; open-balance accounting preserves it.

questions.scenario: Which of these does NOT need a subledger beneath it?
options: Accounts Receivable—Export (many buyers)
Accounts Payable—Import LC (many suppliers)
Share Capital (a handful of shareholders, rarely changing)
Inventory—Yarn (thousands of lots)
questions.explanation: Subledgers earn their keep when detail changes constantly and decisions depend on it (who owes what, which lot is where). Share capital is stable and reported as a single figure — a register suffices.
wrongExplanations: Buyer-wise aging is essential for collections — needs full subledger.
LC-wise supplier debt drives import compliance — needs full subledger.
Lot-wise quantity/value is the inventory subledger itself (Module 5-6 build on it).

questions.scenario: Rafiq asks: 'Can the posting API write the GL entry first and update the subledger a few seconds later?' Best answer:
options: Yes — speed matters more than order
No — both layers must be written in ONE atomic transaction; partial writes create exactly the mismatches this module warns about
Yes, if the delay is under a minute
Subledgers should be rebuilt nightly from the GL instead
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the software translation of 'one event writes both layers.' A crash between the two writes manufactures a mystery like the ৳30 lakh gap — except nobody would know when it happened.
wrongExplanations: Speed never justifies inconsistency; databases do both in milliseconds anyway.
Any window of inconsistency is a window for unexplainable mismatches.
Rebuilding detail FROM summaries is backwards — documents feed detail, detail feeds summaries.

questions.scenario: Nasrin proposes: 'When a buyer overpays, just adjust their oldest invoice upward.' Why is this dangerous?
options: It isn't — balances still match
It falsifies invoice history: the real document trail (invoice amounts, receipts) stops matching records, breaking claims, audits, and buyer reconciliations
It makes aging reports too clean
Overpayments should be deleted instead
questions.explanation: Overpayments belong as their own row (advance/credit note) applied properly later. Editing invoices to absorb them means your records no longer match the signed documents — fatal in any dispute.
wrongExplanations: Balances may match while DOCUMENTS don't — the mismatch just moved to a more dangerous layer.
Clean-but-false reports are worse than messy-but-true ones.
Deleting money movements is never acceptable — everything is kept, classified, and offset properly.

questions.scenario: Shirin's daily routine includes: 'Σ(AR subledger buyer rows) vs 1310 balance'. What is she performing and why daily, not monthly?
options: A trial balance — required only at year-end
Reconciliation of control account to subledger — catching broken postings within a day, when they're one click away instead of buried in a month
Depreciation calculation
An NBR tax filing
questions.explanation: Daily reconciliation localizes errors: yesterday's few transactions are searchable. Monthly discovery means auditing thousands of rows — and possibly having published wrong interim numbers.
wrongExplanations: Trial balance checks debits=credits globally (Module 1); this is the layer-vs-layer check.
Depreciation lives in Module 10 and has nothing to do with AR.
NBR filings have their own schedules; this is internal control.

questions.scenario: The bank asks Shirin for the receivable figure for a loan file, but today's reconciliation hasn't run yet. Most professional response:
options: Send whichever number is smaller to look prudent
Run/complete the reconciliation first, then send the confirmed figure with the reconciliation attached
Send last year's figure
Refuse to give any number ever
questions.explanation: Numbers travel WITH their reconciliation. That habit — evidence attached to every summary — is what separates professional finance from hopeful guessing, and it's exactly what auditors and banks reward.
wrongExplanations: Conservatism doesn't justify presenting unreconciled data.
Stale numbers misrepresent today's position.
Refusing entirely is unnecessary — just finish the check first; it takes minutes when done daily.
